newsitem.title: USA: Stocks in bankrupt, dormant or lost companies may have value.
newsitem.headline: Stocks in bankrupt, dormant or lost companies may have value.

text.p: For some reason, you now own stock in a company that is bankrupt, shut down or untraceable. But your investment -- or at least the antique stock certificate you found among your dead relative's papers -- may not be entirely worthless.
The company may have merely changed names, been acquired, gone private -- or is now back in business after decades of dormancy. It pays to find out.

"The rule here is never assume" it's worthless, said Pierre Bonneau, chief executive of Stock Search International Inc. (800-537-4523), a firm in Tucson, Ariz., that helps clients get to the bottom of such puzzles.
"People either find those old stocks in their grandparents' belongings, cleaning estates, or were given them by their parents. Should they throw them away, keep them, exchange them or frame them?"

Throughout its 28 years, Stock Search has unearthed the story behind 97 percent of the cases it handled, Bonneau said. Value was found in about 15 percent to 20 percent of all searches, with half of these leading to the recovery of $500 to $85,000 for each stock or bondholder.

While the other half was not entitled to payments, the certificates turned out to worth about $10 to $200 each to collectors. This may not seem like much, but scripophily, the hobby of collecting antique stock and bond certificates, is growing rapidly and you never know what they might be worth in the future. Neither did your ancestors.
A share of the long-dead Bank of North America issued in 1873 -- the earliest known printed stock certificate issued by a U.S. company -- fetched a record $33,000 at auction in 1995.

Bonneau's mother, Micheline Masse, founded Stock Search in Montreal in 1969 after discovering that some of the "useless" stock and bond certificates that friends gave her to paper a wall were worth real money. The company moved south of the border when it turned out that most of Masse's clients were Americans.
"It's an unserviced need," said Bonneau, who took over the business in July. "Brokers are too busy" to take the extra step to research an unlisted stock, he said.
Companies generally do not issue stock certificates now unless requested, but a document proving ownership will do if you want to find out whether your investment has any value.

Often small companies that change names, merge or are acquired fail to inform brokers, or their notifications somehow get lost in the system. These corporations may "disappear" from stock exchanges, but investors still retain their original equity, Bonneau noted.
Bonds and shares of companies that are taken over can be exchanged for new ones, as there is no statute of limitations unless the company sets a deadline, which is highly unusual.
Bankrupt companies can leave funds behind for investors to claim once the liquidation process is completed.

In addition, dormant, or even defunct companies can be reactived under different names when market conditions are favourable, injecting new value into your "worthless" securities. This often happens with Canadian mining and oil companies, which hibernate when market prices are too low to justify output.
"That's what happened to gold in the 1970s. Prices jumped and a lot of those companies came back to life. It could be five to 40 years later," Bonneau said.

The North European Oil Corp., an ailing penny-stock company in the 1930s, was reactivated under a new name in 1957 when oil was discovered on surrounding properties, Bonneau said. For every $100 originally invested, shareholders can now claim $130,000. There are still one million shares outstanding held by people who think their shares are worthless, he said.

But how would you know? The company or you may have moved, leaving you in the dark. Even with companies whose operations have not been disrupted, their communication with investors may have been disrupted, as often happens.

For a fee of $85 or lower, Stock Search will start a search that could lead to municipal and state records and other avenues that your attorney or stockbroker may have no time or knowledge to conduct.
"Often a company doesn't have a physical location. It might take two to three weeks of calling to find out the actual situation vs. what the book says," Bonneau said.

If your securities are worth something, Stock Search will recover the money for a 30 percent fee. If they are worthless, the firm will appraise your documents as collectibles and may offer to buy them to resell in its catalogues or two annual mail bid auctions.
Louise Johnson of Escondido, Calif., said Stock Search helped her late husband recover $7,440 in a dollar mutual fund that was liquidated after a complicated international scandal.
"He was tickled pink after all those years," Johnson said. "When you figure that you have something you can't even figure how to cash in and you at least get some money, it was well worth it."
